 The Apple Mac mini M6 may be catching all the headlines right now, but I still think for most people looking for a stylish and powerful mini PC, the Mac mini M4 is the optimal choice. It might lack the extra oomph of the M6, but for daily office tasks and content creation, it's way better value.
 Case in point. The Apple Mac mini M4 is currently $650 (was $799) at Best Buy . If you want a fast, compact desktop for work, photo editing, or everyday use, and you already own a monitor and keyboard, the Mac mini M4 is the best-value Mac you can buy. Meanwhile, Best Buy has the Mac mini M6 for $799 (was $899) .
 • Best for: Professionals and creators upgrading an older Mac or Windows mini PC to a powerful, near-silent desktop without paying M6 prices. .
 • Why we like it: We scored this machine 5 stars in our review, and wondered if it might actually be the best Mac ever. For most people, it will be. Apple’s speedy M4 chip, 16GB of unified memory for smooth multitasking and Apple Intelligence, a tiny five-inch-square design, and handy front-facing USB-C ports and a headphone jack.
 Save $150
 Apple Mac mini M4: was $799 now $649 at Best Buy A compact desktop with Apple’s M4 chip, 16GB of unified memory, and a 256GB SSD, with front USB-C ports and a headphone jack, plus Thunderbolt, HDMI, and Ethernet on the back. It supports Apple Intelligence and comes in silver.
 View Deal 
 Why we recommend it
 In our Mac mini M4 review , our expert Matt awarded it an Editor’s Choice badge and full marks for value, praising its strong performance, much smaller design, and convenient front ports. He called it the cheapest way into the Mac ecosystem, though he noted it struggles with modern games and that its power button sits awkwardly on the underside. Our review unit had a 512GB SSD rather than this model’s 256GB, but it used the same M4 chip and 16GB of memory.
 Price Context & Historical Value
 Apple raised the Mac mini’s starting price to $799 earlier this year as memory costs surged, so this $150 discount is measured against Apple’s real current price rather than an inflated list price. It’s still more than the $599 the M4 Mac mini launched at, and well above the sub-$500 deals we saw before the price hike. Given today’s pricing, though, $649 is a strong deal and a good time to buy.
 For comparison, the Mac mini M6 is currently down to $799 at Best Buy . For some workloads, it may be better. For general office tasks, the M4 is still worth considering for its value.
 Should you buy it?
 ✅ Buy the Apple Mac mini M4 if... you want an affordable, powerful Mac desktop, you already have a monitor, keyboard, and mouse, or you want a near-silent machine for work, photo editing, or music production.
 ❌ Skip the Apple Mac mini M4 if... you need lots of local storage, since 256GB fills quickly; you want to play the latest PC games; or you don’t already own a monitor and accessories, which add to the total cost.

 Mini PCs offer a way to reclaim desk space without giving up the flexibility of a proper desktop. Whether you need an affordable machine for everyday work, a quiet computer for a shared room, a portable powerhouse or a compact gaming setup, there’s now a model to suit.
 Our mini PC expert, Anthony Spadafora, has been using many of the best mini PCs as an alternative to a laptop or a big, bulky desktop for the past seven years, and he's never looked back. The Mac mini M6 is now our top recommendation as the best mini PC, with incredible performance from Apple's chipset in its compact, sleek design. But if you're a fan of Windows, you'll be happy to know there are plenty of fantastic options to choose from today, like the recent Lenovo Yoga Mini .
 Whether you want a mini PC you can slip in your pocket or bag to travel with, something closer to a game console or as much power as possible in a tiny package, there’s something here for every budget and use case. We’ve tested the latest options across real-world use and benchmark workloads to find the mini PCs worth buying today.
 Soon, we'll see Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chips enter the scene, considering these AI-focused processors are aimed at "small desktops." We've tested many RTX Spark laptops and are impressed with the results for local AI tasks, and we'll be going hands-on to see what these RTX Spark compact PCs have to offer, too.
 Why you can trust Tom's Guide 
 There's a lot to test when it comes to testing a mini PC, but here at Tom's Guide we know what we should be looking for. Why? Because we've been at it for 20 year's and our computing team has decades of combined experience. We've got Security and Home Ofiice Editor Anthony Spadafora , who swapped to a mini PC years ago and has never gone back since. Then there's Tony Polanco , Senior Computing Writer, who's been putting PCs to the test through a long and illustrious career at the likes of laptop mag, PC mag, and more.
 Here are the tests we put mini PCs through before they can make this list and get a recommendation.
 We use them as our primary machine. These are computers that you're going to be using for everything, so we want to make sure they're good at it. We swap out our main machines and use them for our heavy workloads. If they can do that, they'll be good for most people.
 We lab test them. We send them to the Tom's Guide testing labs, where they're put through a bunch of stress testing and benchmarks to see just how well they perform.
 We compare them to the competition. There's no point putting them on the list unless they offer a better experience than what we recommend here. So we put them side by side, use them and compare their specs. Is it better? There's a new entry for the list.
 Written by 
 Written by 
 Darragh Murphy 
 Buying Guide Editor 
 In my six years of testing laptops and desktops, my admiration for mini PCs has only grown. If you thought these tiny desktops were just about saving precious space for a minimalist, clean-looking setup (like me), you'll be impressed to learn they come bursting with power and are more than capable of keeping up with demanding workflows and, yes, even the latest PC games. All that in a compact form factor and with the freedom of choosing your go-to mouse, keyboard and monitor? The mini PC revolution has arrived, and we've done all the testing to pick the finest ones around.

 It's been a long time coming, but Apple's Mac mini got a major upgrade, and its standout performance shows it was certainly worth the wait. The Mac mini M6 features Apple's next-gen silicon in a familiar yet hugely welcome sleek and compact design, and it now surpasses the already great Mac mini M4 to become the best mini PC we recommend.
 The Mac mini got a significant performance boost thanks to the 2-nanometer (nm) M6 chip, which translated to a whopping 44% jump over the previous M4 chip in our testing. In fact, despite the M6 being the base chip, it nearly catches up to the pro-level M4 Pro processor, which says a lot considering the price difference between the two. In our tester Anthony's typical daily workload, which involves having dozens of Chrome tabs open along with photo editing, the Mac mini M6 didn't break a sweat.
 Even better? This mini PC is also a hugely capable gaming machine, considering it can play the likes of Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p with 56 fps. Of course, it's better suited for 1080p gaming, but you can get a lot out of gaming on the Mac mini despite it not having a dedicated graphics card.

 The Geekom A5 2025 Edition is our top pick for the best budget mini PC, thanks to its surprisingly affordable price and just how much performance you get for $300. While our previous pick is impressive, the Kamrui E3B , this mini PC is $100 cheaper and just as capable for browsing the web, office work and even some light gaming. Just like with the E3B, Anothny used this refreshed version of the Geekom A5 as his daily driver for a month with a dual-monitor setup, and despite his more demanding workload, it held its own even with a less powerful AMD Ryzen 5 chip, Radeon Vega 7 integrated graphics and 16GB of DDR4 memory.
 In addition to its excellent price-to-performance, Geekom decided to do something different with the A5 by giving it a rose gold colorway instead of the typical silver and black you see on most other mini PCs. It also has a pattern of lined cutouts on either side for extra ventilation, along with a reflective chrome edge up top, which gives it a more premium look overall.  Best Mini PCs: Frequently Asked Questions 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Can a mini PC replace a desktop computer?
 Yes, a mini PC can replace a traditional desktop for web browsing, office work, streaming, video calls and many creative or multitasking workloads, provided you choose hardware that suits the job. 
 For serious PC gaming, GPU-intensive creation or workloads needing lots of expansion, a conventional desktop will still offer better performance and upgrade headroom. That said, mini PCs are only getting more powerful. Be sure to check the processor, graphics, memory, storage, ports and monitor support when choosing.
 Should I buy a Mac mini or a Windows mini PC?
 Buy a Mac mini if you want macOS, use Apple services or software, and value the Mac mini M6’s very strong all-round performance and compact design. 
 Buy a Windows mini PC if you need Windows-only software, want broader game support or prioritise hardware choice, ports and user-upgradeable memory or storage. 
 While we recommend the Mac mini M6 as the mini PC for most, Windows alternatives cover plenty of different needs, for lower-cost, gaming, quiet-operation and workstation-focused needs. 
 Are mini PCs good for gaming?
 Yes, some mini PCs are good for gaming, but the right choice depends on the games, resolution and settings you expect to use. Integrated graphics can suit lighter or less demanding games, while modern AAA games benefit from a model with a capable discrete GPU. That's why we recommend the Minisforum G1 Pro for gaming, because of its desktop-grade Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU.
 You'll find that the G1 Pro reached 45.2 fps in Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p in our tests, and even the Mac mini M6 can reach up to 56.9 fps! That said, you won't find a big selection of games if you opt for a Mac over Windows. 
 Do mini PCs come with a monitor, keyboard and mouse?
 Usually, a mini PC is sold as the computer only, so you will normally need to provide a monitor, keyboard and mouse separately. You may also need to check whether the listed configuration includes storage, memory or an operating-system licence, particularly with more configurable models like the Framework Desktop . 
 Factor those extras into the total cost and confirm that the PC has the ports or wireless connectivity your display and accessories require. Wondering what's worth getting? Check out our guides on the best monitor , best keyboard and best mouse . 
 How much RAM do I need in a mini PC?
 For everyday browsing, office work and streaming, 16GB of RAM is a sensible target; demanding multitasking, creative work, local AI tasks or heavier gaming may justify 32GB or more. 
 RAM cannot always be upgraded later, so consider your likely needs over the life of the PC. Of course, adding extra RAM is getting expensive due to RAMaggedon , so know what you're going to use a PC for to make sure you're not overspending on performance you don't need. 
 Is it worth buying an AI PC?
 An AI PC is worth buying if you intend to use local AI models and agents for complex coding, creative work, repetitive workflows and more with absolute data privacy. For everyday tasks such as researching on the web, writing up documents, replying to emails and gaming, you won't need an AI PC. 
 Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chip is coming to small desktops, and while this chip comes with amazing performance for offline AI work, along with 3D creative work and gaming on a single processor, it's aimed at pro-level users who can take full advantage of its local AI workloads. We asked a tech expert who RTX Spark laptops are for , with Tom Mainelli, Group Vice President of Device & Consumer Research at IDC, stating, "These are outside the budget and needs of mainstream users, for now."
 Many of the mini PCs we recommend are capable of AI work, including the Mac mini M6 and Geekom A9 Max 2026 , but they go beyond just local AI tasks. For general workflows, an AI PC isn't needed. 
 How to choose the best mini PC for you 
 Mini PCs range from small project PCs for under $50 to compact desktops that can cost anywhere between $500 to $1,500 or even more.
 Stick PCs are the most versatile, and generally cost between $100 (£100/AU$150) and $200 (£200/$AU300), and will work with most TVs or monitors, though we don't normally recommend them.
 Mini PC prices vary considerably based on their hardware and come in all sorts of different form factors, but for the most part, the small, rectangular-shaped ones are the most popular, and you won't have a hard time finding one to fit your own particular needs.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Know what you want 
 Finding the right mini PC for you starts with knowing what you're looking for. Do you want something small enough to tuck behind a TV as a dedicated streaming box, or are you looking for something with gaming capabilities? Do you want a basic internet-browsing machine, or do you need serious processing and graphics capabilities?
 Our best picks above do a good job of highlighting the use cases different systems are best suited to, and that should help you narrow down your choices.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Find the right size 
 Then there's the question of form factor. Mini PCs are all small, but there is a range of options within the category, from PCs small enough to slip into your pocket to desktop towers that are still compact enough to stow out of sight.
 You'll sacrifice power for a smaller system, but you can still get a capable desktop that's small enough to carry in a backpack, even if you're after one well-suited for gaming or workstation performance.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Make sure you like your configuration and upgrade options 
 Finally, you want to look at configuration options and upgradability.
 Many mini PCs have two or three configuration options, which can change everything from the amount of included storage to the presence of high-end processors and discrete graphics cards.
 There's also the question of upgrades. Many of the smallest mini PCs leave no room for future hardware changes, but others are designed to let you add memory or storage, or even come outfitted with ports that allow you to attach an external GPU for better graphics and gaming performance.
 When in doubt, check our reviews, which include configuration details and will discuss the potential for future upgrades.

How to upgrade your Mac mini without paying Apple's sky high prices | Macworld 
 When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn't affect our editorial independence .
 by Simon Jary 
 Contributor, Macworld 
 Updated 
 How to upgrade your Mac mini without paying Apple’s sky high prices
 Updated 
 Sep 24, 2026 
 The Mac mini boasts fast processors, and rivals even Apple’s most pro computers despite costing significantly less. However, as great as it is, there is a problem with the Mac mini—the at-purchase storage upgrades are super expensive and after you buy one, it’s nearly impossible to upgrade its internal components. However, we’re here to help.
 There are two basic Mac mini models: the latest M4/M5/M6 mini (5 inches square, 2 inches deep) and older M1/M2 mini (7.7 inches square, 1.4 inches deep). Here, we have rounded up the best hardware upgrades and accessories you can buy for either the old or newer models. Most of the M1/M2 tips work with the Apple Studio, too, as that remains the same size.
 Apple doesn’t let you upgrade the Mac mini with inexpensive third-party components such as RAM or internal storage, and it prices its custom-build options at the very high end of affordability. With the earlier Mac mini Apple fixed the RAM to the processor and the SSD to the logic board so they couldn’t be swapped out after you buy one. The M4/M4 Pro mini is different with a detachable SSD but swapping this out is beyond most mere mortals, and simply not possible with the M5 Pro/M6 Mac mini’s return to soldered NAND storage .
 Here we look at your best Mac mini upgrade options, adding: storage, memory, screen, speakers and microphone. If you want to jump straight to the reviews:
 Hubs and docks for new Mac mini 
 Hubs and docks for Mac mini M2 
 Other Mac mini accessories 
 Above: Inside the Mac mini M4. Although it looks easy, because Apple’s SSD controller is built into the chip, you can’t simply swap out its SSD with a part bought from Amazon or some computer store. If you can do this yourself you probably wouldn’t be reading this article! And it’s impossible on the later M5 Pro and M6 Mac mini. L0vertodream via X 
 Upgrading the Mac mini: Adding memory and storage
 In our FAQ at the foot of this feature we go into more detail about the difficulties of upgrading the Mac mini’s internal components—as it is with most Macs. There are solutions that are quite messy, such as adding external storage. 
 Flexible but messy: A Mac mini with two external SSDs: a Plugable 1TB Thunderbolt 3 External SSD NVMe Drive and a CalDigit Tuff Nano (10Gbps USB-C). Thankfully there are less messy ways of adding fast storage to your Mac mini. Foundry
 Adding external storage
 The simplest way to add storage to a Mac mini is the same as any other Mac: Connect an external hard drive or SSD using one of the Thunderbolt ports on the back of the computer. Even the slowest Solid-state drives (SSD) are faster than mechanical hard disk drives (HDD), but look out for speed differences—entry-level SSDs provide speeds of around 500MBps, while more advanced models can step up to 2,000MBps or even 6,000MBps. See SSD or HDD in the FAQs.
 Another way to add inexpensive portable storage is via an SD or microSD card—once the go-to storage format for camera users but also a great format for cheap and portable backup and archive storage. Sadly, the Mac mini doesn’t have a card reader slot, so you’ll need to add one, such as this UGreen USB-C SD Card Reader for $15.
 But these are admittedly ugly methods. You’ll have wires hanging out of the back of your Mac mini and a desk cluttered with drives. It’s neater to keep storage hidden inside. Apple won’t let you do it, but there are some great solutions that we have tested here.
 Adding internal storage
 The best option is to get more internal storage in your Mac mini, but Apple’s custom-built pricing means upgrading a 256GB model to 1TB will cost you an extra $500, and 2TB will cost $1,000, while M5 Pro options cost even more: 4TB is $1,800 and 8TB will set you back a whopping $3,800.
 If you can’t swing the prices for more storage or just decide later that you need more, there are hardware solutions that connect to the mini without messing up the footprint of the small computer. We’ve tested and reviewed these Mac mini storage accessories for you. The tested Mac mini hubs feature upgradeable and inexpensive internal storage plus a range of extra ports, supporting the NVMe form factors that resemble a stick of chewing gum.
 Installing SSD into Mac mini hub or dock
 Below we review the best Mac mini hubs and docks. Some include a hidden SSD enclosure where you can slot your own storage card with an included screwdriver and sometimes a thermal gel pad to transfer heat away from the drive and into the metal enclosure, preventing the SSD from overheating and suffering from thermal throttling.
 The Satechi CubeDock matched the latest Mac mini (M4/M5/M6) and hides its internal SSD slot under its base. Simon Jary
 For the M4/M5/M6 mini, there are SSD slots in the Ugreen 11-in-1 Mac mini Dock , Satechi CubeDock , Satechi Stand & Hub , and Orico MiniLink , reviewed below. Satechi has an M2 mini version of its Stand & Hub, and you can also choose the OWC ministack STX .
 Installation is simple, with everything bar the SSD board itself included (screwdriver, screws, thermal gel pads). It’s a little fiddly but nothing to be worried about—if you can use a screwdriver, you can install the SSD board yourself.
 SSD types: The docks and hubs we tested all take NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) M.2 SSDs, but check on the appropriate SSD size before investing in the SSD. Some take several lengths—for example 2230, 2242, 2260 and 2280—while others just fit the standard 2280. If that sounds scary, don’t worry as the 2280 is the most common SSD length.
 SSD speeds: Note that the speed of the USB-C or Thunderbolt connection from the dock to the Mac mini will determine the data-transfer rate. A 10Gbps USB-C connection allows an SSD to achieve real-world transfer speeds of around 900 to 1,250 Megabytes per second (MBps). While 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 or USB4 pipes have a theoretical maximum of 5,000MB/s, protocol overhead and enclosure translation typically cap your speeds at around 3,000MBps. An 80Gbps connection (such as Thunderbolt 5) supports real-world SSD speeds of up to 7,000MBps.
 Upgrading the Mac mini: Adding ports and extra expansion
 While the Mac mini has plenty of ports around the back, Apple includes just two USB-C to the front of the M4/M5/M6 mini, and did not bless the M2 Mac mini with any ports at the front at all. Alongside the SSD slots, all of the hubs and docks tested and reviewed here include an array of ports, including USB-A (missing from the M4 mini) and SD/MicroSD card readers (missing from the M2 and M4/M5/M6 Mac mini).
 Thunderbolt , USB-C , Ethernet and HDMI are all included in the Mac mini. Having access to more Thunderbolt or USB-C is useful, especially if powered. Some docks feature faster Ethernet.
 USB-A is the legacy port missing from the Mac mini M4, used mainly for flash drives, memory sticks and older devices. This has largely been replaced with USB-C, but having at least one at your disposal can be handy.
 SD card readers are also missing from the Mac mini, and are an affordable way of adding ultra-portable storage cards, which are cheaper—but slower—than SSDs. You can buy a SanDisk memory card with 512GB of storage for under $100 .
 Another port-adding option is to buy yourself a Thunderbolt hub , such as the 40Gbps CalDigit Thunderbolt 4 Element Hub that features four 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 ports (including one side-mounted upstream to the computer), four 10Gbps USB-A ports, and a power supply. The Element 5 Hub from the same company offers four Thunderbolt 5, two 10Gbps USB-C and three 10Gbps USB-A ports. We’ve tested the best Thunderbolt hubs and docks if you want even more ports than that. Granted, they won’t be as neat as the dedicated Mac mini docks and hubs reviewed here, but there are tons of options out there.
 Best Mac mini hubs and docks
 The criteria we used for the products reviewed below was that they had to fit the Mac mini and connect to it without ruining the Apple aesthetic or the Mac mini’s compact footprint. We tested the following docks and hubs with the Apple Mac mini (M4/M5/M6 models).

 Apple HomePod mini review

 FAQ 
 1. 
 Can you upgrade the Mac mini hard drive?
 It is possible to swap out the internal SSD on some Mac mini models (M4/M4 Pro) but you’ll need to be very tech-savvy. You have to carefully pry open the bottom cover, remove the internal fan, swap the SSD module using Torx bits, and use a second Mac via DFU mode to restore the operating system. Note that opening the chassis voids your Apple warranty and risks damaging delicate internal connectors. Instead, we recommend you look at the add-on solutions reviewed here.
 Apple soldered the solid-state drive (SSD) directly onto the logic board of the older M1/M2 and M5/M6 Mac mini models when you chose the capacity at the point of purchase. While it is not possible to later upgrade the drive, you can add extra SSDs or hard-disk drives (HDD) via accessories.
 2. 
 Can you upgrade the Mac mini memory?
 Apple builds the RAM directly as part of the processor of the Mac mini (unified memory architecture) when you choose the amount of memory at the point of purchase. It is not possible to later upgrade the RAM, so you must choose the most you are likely to need when buying the computer.
 3. 
 SSD or HDD?
 Solid-state drives (SSD) have no moving parts. Data is stored on interconnected flash memory microchips, which allows for data to be pulled from many different places at once and significantly increases memory read speeds. Hard disk drives (HDD) rely on spinning metal disks to read and write data.
 Most of the solutions reviewed here are focused on the faster NVMe type of SSD that speed up boot times, improve the responsiveness of your programs, and generally make your computer feel faster. However, you’ll pay more money for the same storage capacity on SSDs as HDDs. SSDs cost more per gigabyte than mechanical HDDs and aren’t often available in ultra-high capacities. Even as prices of SSDs continue to drop, HDDs will always be cheaper.
 4. 
 Upgrading the Mac mini: Adding faster ethernet
 One of the build-to-order options offered by Apple is to upgrade the Mac mini’s ethernet from 1 Gigabit to 10 Gigabit (an extra $100). As with the RAM and storage, once you’ve picked your Ethernet speed, there’s no way to upgrade the internal connector later. But you can buy adapters quite cheaply. Cable Matters sells a  10G Ethernet Adapter  for around $89 if you suddenly need faster network access after you’ve purchased your Mac mini. Ugreen has  2.5GbE  and  5GbE  adapters that connect to one of your Mac’s USB-C or Thunderbolt ports.
 5. 
 Does the Mac mini see an SSD in a dock as internal or external storage?
 An SSD installed inside a dock is still external storage from the Mac’s perspective.

 So, leaving aside the jump from 256GB to 512GB – which is just ridiculously bad value at 0.78 US dollars or pounds per gigabyte extra – you're generally paying 30-40 cents/pence per GB.
 How does that compare to third-party storage? Not well.
 Our best SSD buying guide lists nine options, that have all been thoroughly tested and TechRadar-approved.
 Number one in the list, the Samsung 990 Pro , currently costs $100/£90 for 1TB – which works out at around 10 cents / 9 pence per GB. Jump up to the 4TB model and the price per GB drops to 7.5 cents, or 6 pence.
 Factor in that the 990 Pro is one of the most expensive options and you can see the difference here – it's roughly a quarter of the price of going direct with Apple.
 The flipside is that you will need to buy an external enclosure too, but these are not expensive.
 And nor do you need to worry about it being a difficult installation process. The most complicated thing about all of this, if you're not particularly techie, is simply the terminology around it all.
 The solution: What you need to buy
 (Image credit: Future) You have two options for upgrading your Mac mini's storage: a portable SSD or an internal SSD plus an external enclosure .
 The former is simpler, in that you just buy one off the shelf and plug it in to a port on the mini, but they're generally more expensive per GB and almost certainly slower.
 Still, if you want to take your storage on the road with you, this might be your best bet; our guide to the best portable SSDs has plenty of options.
 I took the other route, which involved buying an internal SSD and a separate enclosure, or case, to put it in; I'll go into details on that below.
 This has the advantage of being fast enough to rival the mini's internal SSD – well, so long as you buy the right one.
 Know your ports
 (Image credit: Future) If you're coming to the Mac mini M4 from a MacBook, the ports on offer will be a welcome surprise: you get two USB-C 3 ports and a 3mm headphone socket on the front, plus three Thunderbolt 4 / USB-C 4 ports, HDMI and Ethernet on the rear.
 Jargon buster
 M.2: The SSD's form factor; small, rectangular, like a stick of gum
 NVMe: The SSD type; massively faster than the older SATA
 PCie 4.0: The interface bus standard the SSD will connect to. For the fastest speeds this would be 4.0, but the older 3.0 will also do just fine
 Thunderbolt 4: The connectivity standard used by the Mac mini 4's rear ports. It can charge devices, handle two 4K displays and transfer data via USB
 USB 4: The USB protocol used by Thunderbolt 4, enabling speeds of up to 40Gb/s 
 USB 3.2: The previous generation of USB standard has a maximum speed of 10Gb/s. The mini's two front USB-C ports have this spec
 External storage can plug into any of those five USB-C ports, but you'll get the fastest speeds from the Thunderbolt 4 options on the rear. These use USB 4, and have a maximum data transfer speed of 40Gb/s, compared to 10Gb/s for the front ports.
 (The Mac mini M4 Pro, meanwhile, has Thunderbolt 5, which can handle up to 120Gb/s. That's arguably overkill, but then so is the CPU…)
 Theoretically, the absolute fastest speeds will come from an SSD that can take advantage of USB 4 – look for SSDs listed as PCIe 4.0 or 'Gen4', with above 7,000MB/s read and 6,000MB/s write. The Samsung 990 Pro mentioned above is one such SSD.
 That said, you won't get those kind of speeds in real-world use, due to USB 4's 40Gb/s limit. You could therefore buy a cheaper PCIe 3.0 card such as the Samsung 970 EVO Plus. It might be a tiny bit slower than a 4.0 SSD, but you won't notice it outside of benchmarks.
 In terms of form factor and type, meanwhile, there's a dizzying array of jargon associated with SSDs – but there's no need to be confused by it all.
 Simply make sure you buy an M.2 NVMe SSD, ideally Gen4 / PCIe 4.0 if you can afford it , and all will be well.
 The enclosure
 Once you've chosen your SSD you'll need something to put it into. It is technically possible to upgrade the Mac mini's internal storage, but this would void your warranty, and given how easy it is to use an enclosure I'm not sure it's worth it.
 There are dozens of suitable enclosures for SSDs, but all simply provide a home for the storage to slot into, plus a cable to connect to a USB port.
 Some have active cooling fans, some use passive cooling; given that the Mac mini is almost silent, I hated the idea of spoiling that quiet, so went with a passive option.
 Once again, you'll need to ensure the enclosure can handle the speed of your SSD and then transfer that speed to the Mac.
 Therefore, searching for 'M.2 enclosure' will not suffice – you might end up with something that only works with USB 3.2.
 Instead, you specifically need an M.2 NVMe USB 4 or Thunderbolt 4 enclosure . You can use USB 3.2 if you want, but you'll be limited to about a third of the speed.
 What I bought
 (Image credit: Samsung) SSD: Samsung 990 Pro M.2 NVMe 4TB 
 In terms of the SSD, I ended up buying the Samsung 990 Pro M2 NVMe in its 4TB guise. This cost me £257 – which works out at 6 pence per GB.
 This is definitely overkill for the Mac mini M4, in that I'm only getting about half of its potential speed, with USB 4 being the bottleneck.
 However, I figured that I may well upgrade the Mac in the next couple of years, and if I do the Samsung SSD can come along for the ride. Plus, we gave it 5 stars in our Samsung 990 Pro SSD review , so it would seem rude not to pick this.
 As I said above, you could spend less on a PCIe 3.0 SSD and not lose too much in terms of performance. Either way, you will definitely save money over taking the Apple upgrade.

 You'll need to remove a couple of screws, then slide off the bottom of the case to reveal the NVMe slot inside. Remove one more screw, insert the SSD, push down to make contact with the thermal pads, put the screws back in and you're away.
 The whole thing takes about five minutes, max; it's really not a complicated process.
 Next, you'll need to hook it up to one of the Thunderbolt 4 ports on the back of the Mac mini, then format the drive for use.
 Make sure you choose APFS, unless you want to also use it with Macs running an older version of macOS (in which case go for Mac OS Extended) or Windows (ExFAT, generally).
 (Image credit: Future) Performance gains
 (Image credit: Future) Any SSD will be fast enough for most people, particularly if you're used to an old-school hard drive. However, if you're going down the external route rather than buying an Apple upgrade, you'll want your solution to be at least comparable to the internal SSD.
 It's worth noting that the SSDs in Apple's mac Mini M4s vary in speed depending on the size; the 512GB SSD is about 30% faster than the 256GB model, according to discussions on Reddit at least, and the 1TB model is faster still.
 I'm only using the 256GB model, of course, and get a speed of around 2,000 MB/s write and 2,800 MB/s read, based on BlackMagicDesign's Disk Speed Test.
 The Samsung 990 Pro plus OWC 1M2 combo, meanwhile, gives me 3,100 for both write and read – so, slightly faster than the internal SSD.
 Nor does it get too hot. The 1M2 does a fantastic job of keeping it cool whilst in use, and while you can feel it heating up, it's never uncomfortably warm.
 (Image credit: Future) In real life, the difference in speed between the internal and external drives is irrelevant; either one can copy a 5GB file in a matter of seconds. But psychologically, it's great – not only have I saved myself at least £400, but I've even improved the performance, too.
 The result is that I can treat my external storage almost as if it's internal. I have folders on it, I have applications running from it, I have lots and lots of music and photos stored on it – and I'd never know it wasn't sitting inside the Mac mini itself if I didn't look at it.  Mac mini SSD Upgrade: Internal Storage or External SSD?
 By Engin Buldak Published October 30, 2026 Live figures, as of Nov 3, 2026, 9:17 AM UTC 8 min read 
 The easiest way to add storage to a Mac mini is an external SSD over Thunderbolt or USB-C. Apple sells the internal SSD only at purchase in fixed sizes, up to 2TB on the Mac mini with M6 and up to 8TB with M5 Pro. On the 2026 model the SSD is soldered, according to Macworld, so a later internal upgrade is not an option. 
 This guide covers what Apple allows for Mac mini storage, which ports an external SSD can use, how to format it, use it for Time Machine or even start up from it, and what external SSDs cost per TB right now. The information comes from Apple's tech specs and support pages, Apple's warranty terms and reporting by Macworld and MacRumors. ratioDB does not test drives itself. We compare prices and spec sheets. Live amazon.com prices are further down (as of Nov 3, 2026 at 9:17 AM UTC).
 Can I upgrade the SSD in a Mac mini?
 Not on the 2026 Mac mini with M6 or M5 Pro. According to Macworld on September 23, 2026, the SSD is soldered again, based on a teardown by the upgrade company Expand Mac mini. On the previous M4 model the SSD was a removable module, Macworld says. Apple itself only offers more storage at purchase. 
 Apple announced the new Mac mini on August 25, 2026, according to MacRumors, and it has been in stores since September 22, 2026. In its tech specs, Apple lists a base SSD for each model and larger SSDs you can choose when you buy:
 Model SSD as standard configurable at purchase 
 Mac mini with M6, entry model 256GB 512GB, 1TB or 2TB 
 Mac mini with M6, other models 512GB 1TB or 2TB 
 Mac mini with M5 Pro 512GB 1TB, 2TB, 4TB or 8TB 
 So when you buy a Mac mini, plan your storage up front. Anything you need later gets added externally. For the 2024 Mac mini with M4, third parties such as Expand Mac mini sell replacement SSD modules. Apple's warranty, however, does not cover damage caused by service, upgrades or expansions performed by anyone other than Apple or an Apple Authorized Service Provider. Weigh that before any such upgrade.
 Which ports does the Mac mini have for external SSDs?
 Every 2026 Mac mini has 3 Thunderbolt ports in USB-C format on the back, according to Apple: Thunderbolt 4 at up to 40Gb/s on M6 and Thunderbolt 5 at up to 120Gb/s on M5 Pro. The front has 2 USB-C ports with USB 3 at up to 10Gb/s. 
 The ports according to Apple's tech specs:
 Port Mac mini with M6 Mac mini with M5 Pro 
 Back, 3 ports Thunderbolt 4, up to 40Gb/s Thunderbolt 5, up to 120Gb/s 
 USB 4 on the same ports up to 40Gb/s up to 40Gb/s 
 Front, 2 ports USB-C with USB 3, up to 10Gb/s USB-C with USB 3, up to 10Gb/s 
 For a fast external SSD, use the back ports. An SSD with USB 3.2 Gen 2 (10Gbps) runs just as fast on the front, which works out to at most 1,250 MB/s. SSDs with Thunderbolt or USB4 need the back ports, otherwise the front port limits them to 10Gb/s. The USB names are explained in the guide USB 3.2 Gen 2 explained , and what Thunderbolt SSDs offer in the guide Thunderbolt SSD.
 Which external SSD works best with a Mac mini?
 For photos, documents and backups, a USB-C SSD with 10Gbps is enough. For large video projects or as a working drive, an SSD with Thunderbolt or USB4 is worth it. Capacity matters most: plan for what you want to store over the next 2 to 3 years.

 How do I format an external SSD for Mac?
 Open Disk Utility, select the SSD, click Erase and choose APFS. Apple recommends APFS especially for SSDs. If you also want to use the SSD with Windows PCs, choose exFAT. Erasing deletes all data on the SSD. 
 In its guide to starting up from an external drive, Apple calls APFS the recommended format, "especially if your storage device is a solid-state drive (SSD)". For traditional hard drives, Mac OS Extended (Journaled) also works. Many external SSDs ship formatted as exFAT so they work on both Mac and Windows. If you only use a Mac, reformatting to APFS is worth it.
 The difference between the formats and when exFAT makes sense is explained in exFAT vs NTFS . For external hard drives on a Mac, see Best external hard drive for Mac .
 Can I use the external SSD for Time Machine?
 Yes. According to Apple, Time Machine backs up to external drives connected directly over USB or Thunderbolt and to network storage (NAS). The preferred format is APFS or APFS Encrypted. If the SSD uses another format, Time Machine offers to erase and reformat it. 
 Apple says Time Machine can also use a single partition of a drive. A drive formatted for Windows can be converted, but that erases all data on it. Backups to iPhone or iPad are not possible.
 A backup belongs on its own drive, separate from your working files. If one SSD holding both fails, you lose the original and the copy at the same time. How to back up properly is covered in the guide 3-2-1 backup rule . For backups alone, an inexpensive external hard drive is often enough, see external 2.5-inch hard drives .

 The steps according to Apple:
 Connect: Plug the SSD into a compatible port, but not the DFU port. Apple's guide for your model shows which one that is.
 Format: Erase it as APFS in Disk Utility.
 Install macOS: Download macOS and choose the external SSD in the installer, using Show All Disks if needed.
 Select the startup disk: Set the external SSD as your startup disk.
 Apple points out 2 limits: a macOS installation made this way only works on the Mac model it was installed from. And Background Security Improvements are only available when the Mac starts up from its built-in storage. For most people it is simpler to keep macOS on the internal SSD and put apps and files on the external one.

 Frequently asked questions about Mac mini storage
 Is the SSD in the 2026 Mac mini soldered?
 Yes, according to Macworld on September 23, 2026. The report is based on a teardown by the upgrade company Expand Mac mini. On the previous M4 model, Macworld says, the SSD was a removable module.
 How much storage can I choose for a Mac mini?
 According to Apple's tech specs, up to 2TB on the Mac mini with M6 and up to 8TB on the Mac mini with M5 Pro. The entry M6 model has 256GB, all other models 512GB.
 Which port is fastest for an external SSD?
 On the Mac mini with M5 Pro, the Thunderbolt 5 ports on the back at up to 120Gb/s according to Apple. On M6, the Thunderbolt 4 ports on the back at up to 40Gb/s. The USB-C ports on the front reach up to 10Gb/s.
 Does replacing the SSD void the warranty?
 Apple's warranty terms exclude damage caused by service, upgrades or expansions performed by anyone other than Apple or an Apple Authorized Service Provider. An external SSD does not affect the warranty.
 What format does an external SSD need on a Mac?
 Apple recommends APFS, especially for SSDs. If you also want to use the SSD with Windows PCs, exFAT is the choice, because both systems can read and write it.
 Can I move my Photos library to the external SSD?
 Yes. According to Apple, this works with a USB or Thunderbolt drive formatted as APFS or Mac OS Extended (Journaled). You can't use a drive that holds Time Machine backups. Connect the SSD before you open Photos.
 Is an external hard drive enough instead of an SSD?
 For Time Machine and archives, yes, a hard drive usually costs less per TB. For projects you work on directly, an SSD is much faster.

 Yes, the 2024 M4 Mac mini’s internal SSD module can be removed and replaced. Apple’s repair documentation identifies the SSD module as a serviceable part, and independent teardown work confirms that it is physically removable. But this is not a normal M.2 upgrade: a standard NVMe SSD will not work in the internal slot, the replacement must match the exact Mac mini model, and the computer may need to be restored or configured through DFU tools afterward.
 For most owners, an external USB4 NVMe drive is the safer and more flexible way to add storage. Internal replacement is best treated as an advanced repair project—not a routine plug-and-play upgrade.

 What “upgradeable” means for the M4 Mac mini 
 There are three different claims behind the word upgradeable :
 Physically removable: yes. Apple’s 2024 Mac mini repair documentation includes an SSD Module procedure, and Apple lists the SSD module among supported service parts for this model. See Apple’s 2024 Mac mini repair documentation and parts-support information .
 Replaceable with another compatible module: technically yes. Independent repair documentation demonstrates that the module can be removed and replaced.
 Upgradeable with any ordinary M.2 SSD: no. A typical Samsung, Crucial, Western Digital, or other M.2 NVMe drive is not a direct replacement for the internal module.
 That distinction matters. The M4 Mac mini is more serviceable than many earlier Apple silicon Macs, but “serviceable” does not mean Apple has turned its internal storage into a user-upgradeable PC-style drive bay.

 Why a standard M.2 NVMe SSD will not work internally 
 The removable storage board looks similar to an M.2 module, but its architecture is different from a conventional retail NVMe SSD. According to iFixit’s M4 Mac mini SSD replacement guide , the removable board does not contain the usual standalone storage controller.
 Apple integrates the storage controller into the Apple silicon system-on-chip. As a result, the internal module is designed to work with the controller and architecture of the Mac mini’s logic board. A generic M.2 NVMe drive brings its own controller and expects a conventional PCIe/NVMe connection, so it cannot simply be inserted into the Mac mini’s internal connector.
 In practical terms, do not interpret a listing for a “Mac mini M4 M.2 SSD” as permission to buy any standard M.2 drive. For an internal replacement, you need a purpose-built, Mac mini-compatible module—or a module that has been verified as technically equivalent for the exact machine. A normal M.2 SSD is appropriate inside an external USB4 enclosure, but not as a direct internal replacement.
 M4 and M4 Pro modules are not interchangeable by default 
 The 2024 Mac mini is sold with either the M4 or M4 Pro chip. Apple’s published configurations offer the M4 with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, or 2TB of SSD storage. The M4 Pro starts at 512GB and can be configured with up to 8TB. These are factory configuration options, not a guarantee that Apple supports arbitrary aftermarket upgrades. The specifications are documented in Apple’s 2024 Mac mini technical specifications .
 The two versions also differ physically. iFixit reports that the M4 Pro storage module is longer and positioned differently, with differences in clearance and mounting. Therefore:
 Identify whether the computer is an M4 or M4 Pro before buying a replacement.
 Match the module to the exact model and board layout, not merely to the phrase “M4 Mac mini.”
 Do not assume that an M4 Pro module will fit an M4 machine, or vice versa.
 Confirm capacity, connector, mounting points, firmware compatibility, and return terms with the seller before opening the computer.
 Specialist vendors advertise replacement modules, but capacity, stock, compatibility claims, pricing, and reliability are volatile. Vendor-published limits or installation instructions should not be presented as Apple specifications.
 What the internal replacement involves 
 The procedure has two separate challenges: the physical repair and the post-repair software configuration.
 1. Back up before opening the Mac mini
 Assume that the replacement will erase the internal drive. Create a complete, tested backup before beginning. A Time Machine backup is useful, but important files should also be accessible from another location if possible. Confirm that you can retrieve documents, application data, credentials, and encryption or recovery information before disconnecting anything.

 2. Disassemble the computer carefully
 The SSD module is not accessible from the outside. You must open the Mac mini and remove enough components to reach the storage board. This requires suitable precision tools, careful handling of connectors and shielding, and a clean, static-conscious work area.
 Use Apple’s repair manual and the model-specific iFixit guide together. Do not rely on a generic Mac mini teardown: the M4 and M4 Pro layouts and module dimensions differ.
 Keep track of screws and their locations. Damage to a cable, connector, shield, or board can turn a storage upgrade into a much more expensive logic-board repair.
 3. Install a model-matched module
 Replacement is not just a matter of capacity. The module must be electrically and physically compatible with the Apple silicon storage controller in the computer. A module that fits the connector may still fail to initialize, boot, or restore.
 Specialist replacement modules exist, but the market is smaller than the market for ordinary M.2 drives. Check the seller’s model designation, capacity claims, installation instructions, warranty and return policy, and reports from buyers using the same M4 or M4 Pro configuration.
 4. Expect a restore or configuration step
 After the physical replacement, the Mac mini may not simply boot into macOS. Independent repair coverage describes using another Mac and Apple’s restore or configuration tools, with the upgraded Mac mini placed into DFU mode. A restore can erase the machine and reinstall or configure macOS.
 Plan for access to:
 a second compatible Mac;
 a suitable data-capable USB-C cable or other connection required by the restore workflow;
 an internet connection and enough time to download and install macOS;
 your Apple Account credentials and backup;
 a way to troubleshoot or return the replacement module if it is not recognized.
 The exact Apple configuration workflow and supported tool versions can change. Follow the current Apple instructions for the specific repair rather than treating an independent video or seller guide as authoritative. A second Mac is not an optional convenience if the chosen restoration method depends on it.

 For a desktop setup, an enclosure can sit beside the Mac mini or be combined with a compatible stand or dock. Some M4 Mac mini hubs and stands include an M.2 NVMe bay, but verify the exact 2024 M4 or M4 Pro compatibility, port standard, thermal design, drive length, and whether the required USB4 cable is included before purchasing. Accessory designs and listings change frequently.
 Can you move the Home folder to external storage?

 The external drive must remain connected for normal access to the user account.

 The external volume still needs its own backup.

 For many people, a simpler arrangement is to leave macOS and applications on the internal drive and place large libraries, project files, virtual machines, media, or archives on the external SSD. Keep adequate free space on the internal drive for macOS, updates, caches, and normal operation.

 Apple’s Self Service Repair program is intended for people with the knowledge and experience to repair electronic devices, and Apple describes it primarily for out-of-warranty repairs. Apple also states that third-party parts and repairs performed with third-party parts are not covered by the Apple product warranty or AppleCare plan. Review Apple’s current repair terms and Self Service Repair guidance before proceeding.
 That does not justify the overly broad claim that every modification automatically voids every part of a Mac’s warranty.  Who should attempt the internal upgrade? 
 Consider it only if all of these are true: 
 You have the exact M4 or M4 Pro model and a verified compatible module.
 You are comfortable opening compact electronics and following a detailed repair manual.
 You have a complete backup and accept that the replacement may require erasing the computer.
 You have access to another Mac and the required restore/configuration equipment.
 You can tolerate downtime, failed firmware configuration, a defective part, or the possibility of repair damage.
 The cost and risk are acceptable compared with buying a larger factory configuration or using external storage.
 If any of those conditions is missing, use external storage or consult a qualified repair provider.
 A decision guide 
 Have you not purchased the Mac mini? Choose the internal capacity you genuinely need at checkout. Apple lists up to 2TB for the M4 and up to 8TB for the M4 Pro in its 2024 configurations.
 Do you already own the base M4 model? Start with a USB4 NVMe enclosure and a suitable NVMe drive. This is the default recommendation for most people.
 Do you specifically need all storage inside the chassis? Treat an internal module replacement as an advanced repair, not a normal upgrade. Verify the exact model and plan the restore before opening the machine.
 Do you need more ports as well as storage? Consider a Mac mini-compatible hub or stand with an M.2 bay, but check thermal and model compatibility carefully.
 Are you comparing a generic M.2 SSD listing? Buy it for an external enclosure only unless the listing clearly identifies it as a purpose-built internal M4 Mac mini module and provides convincing compatibility information.
 Bottom line 
 The M4 Mac mini’s SSD is upgradeable in the narrow technical sense: Apple documents an SSD Module repair, and the module can be removed. But it is not an easy consumer upgrade. The internal board is not a standard M.2 NVMe drive, M4 and M4 Pro modules differ, compatible aftermarket parts are specialized, and a replacement can require a backup, disassembly, DFU mode, a second Mac, and a full restore.
 For most owners, external USB4 NVMe storage delivers the capacity upgrade with far less risk and better future flexibility. Choose an internal replacement only when keeping the storage inside the chassis is worth the additional technical and financial risk.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Can I install a Samsung or Crucial M.2 SSD inside the M4 Mac mini?
 No. A conventional retail M.2 NVMe SSD is not a direct internal replacement because the Mac mini’s storage-controller architecture differs from a standard M.2 drive. Those SSDs can be used in a USB4 NVMe enclosure instead.
 Does the M4 Mac mini SSD upgrade erase the computer?
 Plan as though it will. Independent repair documentation describes a restore or configuration process after replacement, and that process may erase and reinstall macOS. Make and test a complete backup first.
 Can an M4 SSD module be installed in an M4 Pro Mac mini?
 Do not assume so. The M4 Pro module is reported to differ in length, position, clearance, and mounting. Match the replacement to the exact M4 or M4 Pro model.
 Is external USB4 storage fast enough for a Mac mini?
 It can be very fast for external storage. OWC advertises up to 40Gb/s USB4 connectivity and speeds up to 3,189MB/s for the Express 1M2 solution, although actual performance depends on the enclosure, SSD, cable, thermals, filesystem, and workload.
 Will replacing the SSD automatically void the Mac mini warranty?
 That blanket claim is too broad. Apple says third-party parts and repairs using them are not covered by its product warranty or AppleCare plan, and unauthorized work can affect coverage for resulting damage or the repaired component. Check Apple’s current terms before proceeding.
 The Bottom Line 
 The short answer: the 2024 M4 Mac mini’s internal SSD module can be replaced, but it is a specialized repair—not a standard M.2 upgrade. For nearly everyone who needs more space, a USB4 NVMe enclosure is the safer and more flexible solution.

 by Simon Jary

 Our Verdict 
 While five USB-A ports might be considered too many, this dock adds what the Mac mini M4 is missing, and the built-in SSD enclosure enables you to affordably add up to 8TB of fast internal storage to your Mac mini setup.

 What is it?  The Ugreen 11-in-1 Dock with SSD Expansion is a docking station that adds ports otherwise missing from the Apple Mac mini M4, while matching it in looks and compact footprint.
 Who is it for?  Mac mini M4 users who need a flexible way to neatly expand their system’s storage plus get card readers and USB ports not offered by Apple’s mini.
 Who shouldn’t buy it?  This Ugreen dock works only with the M4 Mac mini. If you want faster data-transfer rates, look to a Thunderbolt dock as this unit connects via 10Gbps USB-C that is fast but not peak 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 or 40Gbps TB4.
 Apple’s Mac mini M4 is remarkably compact, but one thing it definitely isn’t is easy or affordable to upgrade. Once you’ve chosen your storage at checkout, you’re locked into it – and Apple’s SSD upgrade prices quickly become eye-watering, rising to thousands of dollars for higher capacities. Read more in our tutorial  How to Upgrade the Mac mini .
 That’s why the Ugreen 11-in-1 Docking Station with SSD Expansion is more compelling as a storage upgrade than as a dock. Its biggest selling point isn’t the extra USB ports or card readers, but the built-in M.2 NVMe SSD enclosure that lets you add up to 8TB of fast storage using a standard SSD at a fraction of Apple’s upgrade prices. It transforms the Mac mini into a system with storage you can expand whenever your needs change.
 The additional ports are almost a bonus. The dock restores USB-A connectivity and adds SD and microSD card readers, all while matching the Mac mini’s footprint so neatly that it looks like part of the computer rather than an accessory.
 Apple’s Mac mini is such an elegant design that placing it on top of a conventional dock feels aesthetically criminal, while also taking up unnecessary desk space. The Mac mini itself offers the essentials – two USB-C ports on the front, three Thunderbolt ports on the back, Gigabit Ethernet and HDMI – but little else.
 There’s no USB-A, and while many users won’t miss it, photographers and videographers may miss having built-in SD and microSD card readers. Ugreen’s Mac mini-matching dock solves both shortcomings while discreetly hiding an SSD enclosure underneath, making it the neatest and most affordable way to expand a Mac mini’s storage without compromising its compact design.
 Simon Jary
 Specs and features: What ports and features does it add?
 One upstream built-in USB-C cable (10Gbps)
 1x USB-C (power input)
 2x USB-C (10Gbps)
 3x USB-A (10Gbps)
 2x USB-A (5Gbps)
 M.2 SSD Enclosure (up to 8TB capacity)
 UHS-I SD card reader (104MBps)
 UHS-I microSD card reader (104MBps)
 USB-C power supply required
 Ugreen calls this an 11-port dock, but there’s really only 10 to play with as the eleventh is required to connect upstream to the Mac mini.
 None of these USB ports can output power to external devices, which is a missed opportunity, as hubs and docks are often convenient for charging other devices such as iPhones, iPads and even MacBooks. However, as the USB-C and Thunderbolt ports on the Mac mini itself can charge at 15W this is less of an issue, although iPhone fast charging requires at least 18W.
 Two of the dock’s USB-C ports are for attaching devices such as storage drives at 10Gbps.
 Ugreen does sell a $299 Thunderbolt 5 Mac mini M4 dock that pushes data transfer bandwidth to 80Gbps. We’ll review that when we’ve got confirmation that it will be available in the U.S. We’ve seen it in the U.K. but strangely not on the other side of the pond.
 A third brings power into the dock itself, which provides power in for the SSD when connected to an external USB-C charger. Alternatively, the dock can draw power from your Mac mini.
 Simon Jary
 The dock has five USB-A ports, which is surely overkill these days. Who has five legacy USB-A devices? If you are forever swapping in and out older thumb drives, then this might be useful. Otherwise, we’d have preferred more USB-C ports, and one with decent charging potential.
 None of the USB ports can be used to connect a monitor. The Mac mini itself can simultaneously support up to three displays—two up to 6K over Thunderbolt and one up to 5K Thunderbolt or a 4K over HDMI—so this is not really an issue. However, if one of the USB-C ports was powerful enough to connect to a display, it might free up one of the Mac mini’s Thunderbolts.
 The company also sells a model with a DisplayPort instead of two of the USB-C ports if you want to use it to add a monitor with that connection.
 Simon Jary
 Is the SSD expansion worth it?
 Adding internal storage to the Mac mini is inflexible and expensive. It must be customized at the point of purchase, and then it’s set. You can add external storage via the Thunderbolt ports but that is a messy solution when you consider the mini’s compact footprint and good looks.
 It’s also ruinously expensive compared to storage you can buy outside of the Apple Store. The base Mac mini M4 comes with 256GB of internal SSD storage. Doubling this via Apple to 512GB will cost you $200, $500 to 1TB, $1,000 to 2TB, $1,800 to 4TB, and $3,800 to 8TB.
 A dock such as this is much cheaper and more flexible.
 Underneath the dock is a screw-off panel that reveals an SSD slot that can take M.2 NVMe SSDs of types 2230, 2242, 2260 and 2280. Maximum capacity is 8TB. Installing an SSD card is pretty easy unless you have giant hands. It comes with a thermal gel strip to help manage temperatures that might otherwise lead to speed throttling.
 Where Apple would charge you nearly $4,000 for 8TB, you can buy an SSD card with the same for under $1,500 or more for the very fastest speeds. An extra 1TB might cost you around $180 , and 2TB for under $300 . Storage prices are volatile, so may be higher or lower when you purchase.
 The flexibility lies in the fact that you can upgrade this to a higher-capacity SSD when required. Note that there is no SSD pre-installed and you’ll need to buy this as an extra.
 The two card readers at the front of the dock support ultra-portable SD and MicroSD cards. You could just use these for backup storage, but at 104MBps UHS-I they are probably too slow to work directly from while the dock’s internal SSD supports up to 10Gbps.
 Simon Jary
 How well does it fit the Mac mini M4?
 The dock is designed and engineered to match the Mac mini M4, and blends seamlessly while adding the port and slot functionality. It sits underneath the mini.
 It connects to the Mac mini via its integrated short 4cm cable, keeping your desk neat and not detracting from the mini’s compact footprint.
 If you find the Mac mini’s power button tricky to reach, the dock’s clever cutout means you can turn it on without lifting it. Anti-slip silicone pads on the bottom add stability on the desk.
 Simon Jary
 Is it good value?
 The Ugreen Mac mini 11-in-1 Docking Station with SSD Expansion is priced at $89.99 / £89.99 , although there were some discounts available at the time of writing. 
 It’s also available from Amazon and Amazon U.K. Check our price comparison table in this review for live pricing.
 For alternative solutions, see our reviews of the best Mac docking stations .
 Should you buy the Ugreen Mac mini 11-in-1 Docking Station?
 The principal reason to consider this dock is its built-in SSD enclosure that enables you to flexibly and more affordably add up to 8TB of fast internal storage to your Mac mini setup.
 The storage card readers are also potentially useful to mini owners as Apple added one of these only to the pro-level Mac Studio. Five legacy USB-A ports is overkill but the two downstream 10Gbps USB-C ports will prove useful.
